message.content:
### Tenant Rights in Texas (as of 2024) Below is a concise overview of the most important rights and protections you have as a tenant in Texas. This list is not exhaustive, but it covers the core legal framework that governs residential leases, landlord‑tenant relationships, and habitability standards. | Area | Key Rights & Protections | Practical Tips | |------|--------------------------|----------------| | **Security Deposit** | • Landlord may charge up to **one month’s rent** for a furnished unit and **two months’ rent** for an unfurnished unit.
• Must be returned within **30 days** after lease ends, minus any lawful deductions. | Keep a copy of the lease, move‑in inspection sheet, and receipts for any repairs you made. | | **Habitability** | • Landlord must keep the premises in a safe, livable condition (plumbing, heating, electrical, structural integrity).
• Must comply with all local building, health, and safety codes. | Document any problems (photos, emails). If unresolved, you may withhold rent or repair and deduct. | | **Rent Payment** | • Rent is due on the date specified in the lease; late fees are allowed only if stated in the lease. | Pay on time or negotiate a payment plan if needed. | | **Lease Termination** | • **Month‑to‑month** tenants can terminate with **30 days’ written notice**.
• Landlords must give **30 days’ notice** to terminate a month‑to‑month lease. | Provide written notice via certified mail or email (with read receipt). | | **Eviction** | • Landlord must provide a **written notice** (30 days for nonpayment, 30 days for lease violation, 60 days for no‑cause termination).
• Eviction can only proceed through the court system. | If you receive a notice, respond promptly. Seek legal counsel if you believe the eviction is unlawful. | | **Privacy** | • Landlord may enter the premises only for **reasonable reasons** (repairs, inspections, showing to prospective tenants) and must give **reasonable notice** (usually 24 hours). | Keep a log of any entries. | | **Discrimination** | • Landlords cannot discriminate based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, familial status, disability, or source of income (e.g., public assistance). | Report violations to the Texas Commission on Human Rights or the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD). | | **Repair and Deduct** | • If the landlord fails to fix a major problem, you may repair it yourself and deduct the cost from your rent, provided you follow the proper procedure. | Keep receipts and notify the landlord in writing before making repairs. | | **Rent Control** | • Texas has **no statewide rent control** laws. | Rent increases must be in accordance with the lease or a new lease agreement. | | **Lease Renewal** | • Landlords cannot unilaterally change lease terms without your consent. | Negotiate renewal terms before signing. | | **Legal Assistance** | • Texas offers free or low‑cost legal aid for tenants (e.g., Texas Legal Services Center, local bar associations). | Contact a local tenant advocacy group if you need help. | #### Quick Reference Checklist 1. **Read Your Lease** – Understand the terms, notice periods, and any special clauses. 2. **Document Everything** – Photos, emails, and written notices help protect you. 3. **Know the Notice Periods** – 30 days for most actions; 60 days for no‑cause termination. 4. **Report Problems Promptly** – Give the landlord a chance to fix issues. 5. **Seek Legal Help Early** – If you receive an eviction notice or suspect discrimination, act quickly. --- ### Where to Find More Information | Resource | What It Offers | |----------|----------------| | **Texas Property Code** | The statutory law governing landlord‑tenant relations. | | **Texas Commission on Human Rights** | Handles discrimination complaints. | | **U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD)** | Federal housing rights and discrimination enforcement. | | **Local Tenant Advocacy Groups** | Free legal advice, mediation services, and tenant education. | | **Texas Legal Services Center** | Free legal assistance for low‑income residents. | --- #### Final Note While this guide provides a solid foundation, laws can change, and local ordinances may add additional protections. If you’re facing a specific issue—such as an eviction notice, a dispute over a security deposit, or a habitability concern—consult a qualified attorney or a local tenant advocacy organization for tailored advice.
